title: Linux boot process
intro: Questions on the Linux boot sequence from power-on to a running login prompt. Understanding the boot process is essential for diagnosing failures, customising kernel parameters, and recovering broken systems.

questions.prompt: What replaced the legacy BIOS on modern PCs, offering faster boot times, Secure Boot support, and native GPT disk awareness?
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**UEFI (Unified Extensible Firmware Interface)** is the modern firmware standard. Key differences from BIOS:
- Supports disks larger than 2 TB (GPT)
- Graphical pre-OS environment
- **Secure Boot** — only signed bootloaders can execute
- Stores boot entries in NVRAM (managed with `efibootmgr`)
- EFI applications (`.efi` files) replace the MBR bootstrap

questions.prompt: What is the name of the default bootloader on most Linux distributions?
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**GRUB2 (GRand Unified Bootloader version 2)** is the standard Linux bootloader. It:
- Reads a configuration file (`/boot/grub/grub.cfg`) to present a boot menu
- Loads the kernel (`vmlinuz`) and initial RAM disk (`initramfs`)
- Passes kernel parameters to the kernel
- Supports chainloading (e.g. dual-booting Windows)

Config is generated by `update-grub` / `grub2-mkconfig` from `/etc/grub.d/` and `/etc/default/grub`.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the temporary filesystem loaded into memory during early boot, before the real root filesystem is mounted?
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**initramfs** (initial RAM filesystem) is a compressed `cpio` archive that the kernel extracts into a tmpfs at boot. It contains:
- Kernel modules needed to mount the real root (e.g. storage drivers, LVM, LUKS)
- A minimal `/init` script that mounts the real root and hands off control

The legacy format was `initrd` (a block device image); `initramfs` replaced it as it is simpler and more flexible.

questions.prompt: What is the PID of the first user-space process started by the Linux kernel?
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**PID 1** is the init process — started directly by the kernel after mounting the root filesystem. On modern systems this is **systemd**. PID 1 is the ancestor of all other processes and is responsible for:
- Starting system services
- Reaping zombie processes
- Handling system shutdown and reboot signals

questions.prompt: What systemd unit type replaces the SysV concept of runlevels?
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Targets** are systemd units that group other units. They map to the legacy runlevels:

| Runlevel | systemd Target |
|---|---|
| 0 | `poweroff.target` |
| 1 | `rescue.target` |
| 3 | `multi-user.target` |
| 5 | `graphical.target` |
| 6 | `reboot.target` |

`systemctl get-default` shows the current default target.

questions.prompt: What systemd target represents a fully operational multi-user system with networking but without a graphical display server?
questions.solutionMarkdown: `multi-user.target` is the standard server boot target — equivalent to runlevel 3. Adding `systemd.unit=multi-user.target` as a kernel parameter boots into this target permanently. Contrast with `graphical.target` (runlevel 5), which additionally starts the display manager.

questions.prompt: What command shows log messages from the current and previous boots managed by the systemd journal?
questions.solutionMarkdown:
`journalctl -b` shows the current boot log. `journalctl -b -1` shows the previous boot. The journal persists across reboots when `/var/log/journal/` exists.

Useful filters:
```bash
journalctl -b -p err     # errors only
journalctl -b -u sshd    # logs for a specific unit
journalctl --since today
```

questions.prompt: What partition, typically formatted as FAT32, stores EFI bootloaders and is required for UEFI boot?
questions.solutionMarkdown:
The **EFI System Partition (ESP)** is a FAT32 partition (type code `EF00`) containing `.efi` bootloader files. On Linux:
- Typically mounted at `/boot/efi`
- Contains `EFI/ubuntu/grubx64.efi` (or distro equivalent)
- `efibootmgr` lists and manages NVRAM boot entries pointing into this partition

questions.prompt: What file, generated by update-grub or grub2-mkconfig, is the active GRUB2 configuration read at boot?
questions.solutionMarkdown:
`/boot/grub/grub.cfg` (Debian/Ubuntu) or `/boot/grub2/grub.cfg` (Red Hat) is the generated config. **Never edit it by hand** — it is regenerated on kernel upgrades. Customise via:
- `/etc/default/grub` — kernel parameters, timeout, default entry
- `/etc/grub.d/` — script hooks for menu entries

questions.prompt: What file can you read on a running system to see the exact kernel parameters that were used at boot?
questions.solutionMarkdown:
```bash
cat /proc/cmdline
# BOOT_IMAGE=/boot/vmlinuz-6.1.0 root=UUID=abc123 ro quiet splash
```
This is useful for verifying that custom parameters (e.g. `iommu=off`, `nomodeset`, `systemd.unit=rescue.target`) actually took effect. The kernel populates this from what GRUB passed at load time.

summaryMarkdown:
## Boot troubleshooting quick reference

| Problem | Where to look |
|---|---|
| System won't boot to GRUB | UEFI NVRAM entries (`efibootmgr`), ESP contents |
| Kernel panic at initramfs | Missing driver in initramfs (`mkinitramfs`) |
| Stuck after kernel loads | Kernel params (`nomodeset`, `acpi=off`) |
| Service fails to start | `journalctl -b -u <unit>` |
| Default target is wrong | `systemctl set-default <target>` |
